title: Yayati's thousand years
hook: a king borrows his son's youth for a thousand years and learns why, to the discerning, even pleasure holds pain
carry: duhkha: feeding desire never puts it out
tomorrow: a born hermit is sent to learn freedom from a king. why a king?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's arrow, karmashaya, and your line: karma, every deed is a seed that ripens. Today, a line that sounds gloomy at first.

King Yayati is cursed with sudden old age. His father-in-law, the sage Shukra, leaves one way out: if a son will take the old age, Yayati can have that son's youth. Four sons refuse. The youngest, Puru, says yes. So Yayati is young again, and the Mahabharata says he enjoys it for a thousand years. Every pleasure a king could want. At the end of it, he calls Puru back.
screen: `A CURSE OF OLD AGE.` → `A SON GIVES HIS YOUTH.` → `A THOUSAND YEARS OF PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: He gives the youth back, and says the line Hindus still quote: desire is never quenched by enjoying what's desired. Like fire fed with ghee, it only grows. Then he goes to the forest. A thousand years, and it wasn't enough, because enough was never coming. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.15: to the discerning, all is duhkha, suffering. It sounds gloomy. It's a diagnosis, and Yayati is the case. Patanjali gives four reasons even pleasure hides pain. Change: the sweet thing is already ending, like borrowed youth. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it. Impressions: each pleasure leaves a groove that wants more, the ghee on the fire. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other. The commentary says most people are like an arm: a thread of wool lands and nothing is felt. The discerning are like the eye, and the same thread hurts. Then the turn, 2.16: heyam duhkham anagatam, the suffering not yet come is to be avoided. And 2.17 names the cause: the seer joined to the seen. Hindus who fast, on Ekadashi, in Navratri, on a weekday for a chosen god, do it first as devotion; many teachers add Yayati's reason: going without a little, on purpose, keeps the fire from growing. Today it's the next order, the next episode, the next scroll. Yayati already ran that experiment, for a thousand years.
screen: `FIRE FED WITH GHEE ONLY GROWS.` · `2.15: TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING.` · `FOUR WAYS PLEASURE HIDES PAIN.` · `AVOID THE PAIN NOT YET COME.` · then, large: `FEEDING DESIRE NEVER PUTS IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want that keeps coming back, a snack, a scroll, one more episode. Feel it rise, like a flame. This once, don't feed it. Watch what the flame does when no ghee comes: it flares, then often settles. If you pray, offer that want to God the way a fasting family offers the day. If you don't, just let it be a small, chosen going-without.
Duhkha, suffering, pain, unease, the opposite of sukha, ease. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.
Your line: duhkha, feeding desire never puts it out. Yayati took a thousand years to learn it. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 454 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A HERMIT SENT TO A KING. WHY?`

howItsDone: Yayati's verse about fire and ghee is quoted across Hindu texts, including the Bhagavata Purana and the Manusmriti. Many Hindus keep fasts such as Ekadashi as devotion and as practice in going without, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline: the illness and its cause, with the cure and remedy to follow.

fork.setup: after a thousand years of every pleasure, Yayati says desire grows like fire fed with ghee. which reason in 2.15 is that?
options: impressions: each pleasure leaves a groove that wants more.
none: the pleasures were just too small.
fork.reveal: samskara, the groove pleasure leaves. feeding it only grows it, so 2.16 turns to the pain not yet come.

original.note: Sanskrit duḥkha: pain, suffering, unease; the opposite of sukha, ease.

vivekin.meaning: the discerning one, who sees clearly
